title: How Buffett reads Kraft Heinz, stock prices, and America's tailwind: CNBC interview, Feb 2019
summary: In a long CNBC interview after his 2018 letter, Buffett explains why Berkshire overpaid for Kraft Heinz, why a good business can't fix a bad price, and why he shrugs off mark-to-market swings. He also covers buying stocks when cheaper, buybacks, index funds, IPOs, Bitcoin, and the American tailwind.

principles.text: Overpaying is permanent: a business earns what it earns regardless of the price you paid.
principles.quote: the business does not earn more just because you pay more for it

principles.text: Judge a business on returns to tangible assets, but your own cost basis includes any premium you paid.
principles.quote: we paid a hundred billion more than the tangible assets so for us it has to earn on 107 and not just on the seven billion that the business employees

principles.text: The market serves you; a price drop matters only if long-term business value changed.
principles.quote: the stock market is there not to instruct me it's there to serve me

principles.text: If you plan to keep owning a business, falling prices help you, especially when the company is repurchasing shares.
principles.quote: we're way better off you know if it's a if it's at a lower price when they're repurchasing share

principles.text: Whether stocks are expensive depends on interest rates; at very low long-term rates, stocks look cheap.
principles.quote: if you tell me that 3% long bonds will prevail over the next 30 years stocks are incredibly cheap

principles.text: Most people should own a low-cost S&P 500 index fund; just betting on America beat any political view.
principles.quote: you do not want to have a political view in investing
